lines.text: AI agents, explained.
This is Kemi. She types one line: find the cheapest flight to Nairobi on Friday, and put it in my calendar.
A chatbot would describe how to do that. An agent goes and does it.
Agent. Tools. Memory. MCP. It sounds like a lot. It's really just one loop. Let's build it from scratch.
Step one. The brain. A language model on its own does one thing. Text in, text out.
It can't check a price. It can't open a calendar. It's a brain in a jar. Smart, but no hands.
Step two. Tools. So we give it hands. A short menu: search flights, read calendar, add event.
Each tool is a name, a description, and the inputs it needs.
Now when Kemi asks, the model doesn't answer. It writes a request: search flights, Lagos to Nairobi, Friday.
Your code runs it, and hands back the result. The model never touches the internet. It just asks. That's a tool call.
And those descriptions matter. For one agent, Anthropic spent more time on the tools than on the prompt.
Step three. The loop. One search isn't enough. The cheapest flight is sold out.
So the model reads the result, and picks the next move. Search again. Compare. Check the calendar.
Think. Act. Observe. Repeat. Anthropic describes agents as a model using tools, in a loop.
But every loop adds more text. And soon, the model starts to forget.
Step four. Memory. A model can only read so much at once. That limit is its context window.
Fill it with old results, and early details get pushed out, like what Kemi actually asked.
So agents keep notes. They summarise old steps, and read them back when needed.
Now, Kemi's agent has three tools. What if it needed three hundred?
Quick thing. Building AI agents is part of the AI track on Teyro.
Okay. Back to the wiring.
Step five. One plug. Before, every app wired every tool by hand.
So in November twenty twenty four, Anthropic released an open standard: the Model Context Protocol. MCP.
Think USB-C, for AI. Build a tool once, and any MCP app can plug it in.
A server offers three things: tools to run, resources to read, and prompts to reuse.
Step six. Guardrails. Searching flights is harmless. Paying for one isn't.
So risky tools need a human. The agent pauses, shows Kemi the flight, and waits for a yes.
The MCP spec says it plainly: get the user's consent before running any tool.
And here's the trap. Most agent failures aren't the model. They're the loop.
Small mistakes stack up. If each step is ninety five percent right, twenty steps in a row come out right only about a third of the time.
And a loop with no exit just keeps going. And spending.
So good agents check real results every step, and have a stop condition. Goal reached, or too many turns.
To be fair, most tasks don't need an agent. One good prompt is often enough.
So. A brain. Tools for hands. A loop to keep going. Notes to remember. MCP to plug in. Guardrails to stay safe. And a way to stop.
No magic. Just a model, some tools, and a loop.
Want to build your own agent? Learn it on Teyro.
